nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name: Eucinostomus argenteus
Common Name: Spotfin mojarra

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Gerreidae

OTHER COMMON NAMES: mojarra ( 8 3 5 ) ; sand perch, mutton minnow (664); silver mojarra (378 581 7 9 1 )

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (378 581 7 9 1 )
	Reference for Classification ( 9 5 6 )

Other: TAXONOMIC NOTE - Matheson and McEachran (1444) separated Eucinostomus harengulus Goode and Bean from the E. argenteus complex. Robins et a1 (956) recognized this distinction and included E. harengulus, the tidewater mojarra, as a separate species in the 1991 Common and Scientific Names list. It is probable that earlier studies of E. gula and E. argenteus included specimens of the now recognized E. harengulus.

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Although not highly regarded, it is marketed fresh in many localities. Made into fish meal in Cuba and used as live bait in the snapper fishery. Mainly caught with beach seines and shrimp trawls, but also with gillnets, trammel nets, traps, and cast nets (791).

Recreational: Not sought by recreational anglers.

Ecological Role: Important as a forage species due to its abundance.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Recorded from New Jersey, where it is found primarily as a stray, to southeastern Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Bermuda (791 835 871 891 1037) . Particularly abundant off south Florida, in the Antilles, and the Bahamas (871) . In the Bahamas, found on both the Little Bahama and Great Bahama Banks (871). Also found in the warm and temperate eastern Pacific (791 871).

Within Study Area: Occurs on both coasts of Florida (835). Christensen (887) considered this species as probably the most abundant of the marine fishes in the Loxahatchee River and at Jupiter Inlet, where he collected it year round. Springer and Woodburn (664) collected the species year-round in Tampa Bay. Reported as the tenth most abundant fish species in a study conducted in Everglades National Park, where it was collected in all months except January (89% of catch taken in summer and fall months) (1373); one of the ten most abundant fish species collected Florida Bay (724 1431 1432). Found throughout Florida Bay, though more abundant in the western than in central or eastern portions of the bay (1431 1432). Studies in the Ten Thousand Islands area also found E. argenteus to be among the top ten species in numbers collected (1054 1443). Also recorded from freshwater springs (1051).

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
A schooling species commonly found in shallow waters (789).

Apparently migrates into the open gulf of Mexico where it has been found in waters as deep as 67.7m (303 664 833 1361). This migration is generally thought to be a spawning migration, although no ripe individuals have ever been collected (664); presumably, the newly hatched young are carried to estuarine waters which they reach as late postlarvae.

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type: Found in shallow salt water and in fresh water streams and rivers, especially spring-runs (664 835). Abundant in tidal streams lined with marsh grasses and/or mangroves (378 1443). Frequently found to be concentrated in open waters and water courses (378). Inhabits freshwater springs (1051). A year round resident of coastal marshes in west central Florida (378). Abundant among mangrove prop roots, and commonly found associated with seagrass beds (724). Spends parts of its life history in protected, low salinity areas, on the Gulf beaches, and in open Gulf waters (664). Springer and Woodburn (664) stated that larger individuals prefer deeper, higher salinity waters offshore to the bays and bayous. Reported to occur in the Gulf of Mexico at depths of 18.3 to 67.7 m (303 833).

Substrate: Collected over open sand bottoms along the Gulf beaches (664). Said to occur mainly on shallow sand flats (791). Frequently found among mangrove prop roots or over seagrass beds (724 1431 1443). Collected more often over seagrass than other bottom types in the Ten Thousand Islands area of Florida (1054).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Collected at Cedar Key at temperatures of 14.5-15.5 C (5811, in Tampa Bay at 12.8-32.5 C (664), from 20.4-31.3 C in Charlotte Harbor (7891, 16.0-34.0 C in Everglades National Park (702 1373), 19.9-33.6 C at Matecumbe Key (8001, and at 18.0-36.0 C at Jupiter Inlet (887). Springer and Woodburn (664) reported that the species was killed by cold (water temperatures of 13 C) in the Tampa Bay area, and that live individuals noted at the same time swam sluggishly. Gilmore et a1 (236) also reported the species suffering from hypothermal stress in Tampa Bay when water temperatures ranged from 6.7 to 7.7 C. Death caused by cold temperatures has been reported at temperatures of 9.6 C in Tampa Bay (1447) and at 6.0 C in Indian River Lagoon (236).

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body: Juvenile/adults: Euryhaline, with a wider salinity tolerance than E. gula (789 891). Said to prefer lower salinities than E. gula by some (664 789 8871, but others found that it prefers higher salinities than E. gula (702 1446). Reported to be more abundant at low to intermediate salinities in the Ten Thousand Islands, and although taken at salinities from 0-35 ppt, the species was much more abundant over the range of 2-20 ppt (1054). Some studies have collected the species primarily in brackish, estuarine waters (378 664), but also reported as the most abundant mojarra in high salinity water in southern Florida (702 1446). This apparent contradiction in salinity preferences may result, in part, from the confused taxonomic status of the species. sections.heading: HEADER
sections.content:
Title: spotfin mojarra (Eucinostomus argenteus)

FLELMR CODE: 1672

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Scientific Name: Eucinostomus argenteus
Common Name: Spotfin mojarra

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum: Chordata
      Class: Osteichthys
      Order: Perciformes
      Family: Gerreidae

OTHER COMMON NAMES: mojarra ( 8 3 5 ) ; sand perch, mutton minnow (664); silver mojarra (378 581 7 9 1 )

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (378 581 7 9 1 )
	Reference for Classification ( 9 5 6 )

Other: TAXONOMIC NOTE - Matheson and McEachran (1444) separated Eucinostomus harengulus Goode and Bean from the E. argenteus complex. Robins et a1 (956) recognized this distinction and included E. harengulus, the tidewater mojarra, as a separate species in the 1991 Common and Scientific Names list. It is probable that earlier studies of E. gula and E. argenteus included specimens of the now recognized E. harengulus.

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  Although not highly regarded, it is marketed fresh in many localities. Made into fish meal in Cuba and used as live bait in the snapper fishery. Mainly caught with beach seines and shrimp trawls, but also with gillnets, trammel nets, traps, and cast nets (791).

Recreational: Not sought by recreational anglers.

Ecological Role: Important as a forage species due to its abundance.

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  Recorded from New Jersey, where it is found primarily as a stray, to southeastern Brazil, including the Gulf of Mexico and Bermuda (791 835 871 891 1037) . Particularly abundant off south Florida, in the Antilles, and the Bahamas (871) . In the Bahamas, found on both the Little Bahama and Great Bahama Banks (871). Also found in the warm and temperate eastern Pacific (791 871).

Within Study Area: Occurs on both coasts of Florida (835). Christensen (887) considered this species as probably the most abundant of the marine fishes in the Loxahatchee River and at Jupiter Inlet, where he collected it year round. Springer and Woodburn (664) collected the species year-round in Tampa Bay. Reported as the tenth most abundant fish species in a study conducted in Everglades National Park, where it was collected in all months except January (89% of catch taken in summer and fall months) (1373); one of the ten most abundant fish species collected Florida Bay (724 1431 1432). Found throughout Florida Bay, though more abundant in the western than in central or eastern portions of the bay (1431 1432). Studies in the Ten Thousand Islands area also found E. argenteus to be among the top ten species in numbers collected (1054 1443). Also recorded from freshwater springs (1051).

Mobility and Migration:

sections.heading: Life Mode
sections.content:
A schooling species commonly found in shallow waters (789).

Apparently migrates into the open gulf of Mexico where it has been found in waters as deep as 67.7m (303 664 833 1361). This migration is generally thought to be a spawning migration, although no ripe individuals have ever been collected (664); presumably, the newly hatched young are carried to estuarine waters which they reach as late postlarvae.

sections.heading: BENTHIC HABITAT
sections.content:
Habitat Type: Found in shallow salt water and in fresh water streams and rivers, especially spring-runs (664 835). Abundant in tidal streams lined with marsh grasses and/or mangroves (378 1443). Frequently found to be concentrated in open waters and water courses (378). Inhabits freshwater springs (1051). A year round resident of coastal marshes in west central Florida (378). Abundant among mangrove prop roots, and commonly found associated with seagrass beds (724). Spends parts of its life history in protected, low salinity areas, on the Gulf beaches, and in open Gulf waters (664). Springer and Woodburn (664) stated that larger individuals prefer deeper, higher salinity waters offshore to the bays and bayous. Reported to occur in the Gulf of Mexico at depths of 18.3 to 67.7 m (303 833).

Substrate: Collected over open sand bottoms along the Gulf beaches (664). Said to occur mainly on shallow sand flats (791). Frequently found among mangrove prop roots or over seagrass beds (724 1431 1443). Collected more often over seagrass than other bottom types in the Ten Thousand Islands area of Florida (1054).

sections.heading: Temperature
sections.content: Juvenile/adults: Collected at Cedar Key at temperatures of 14.5-15.5 C (5811, in Tampa Bay at 12.8-32.5 C (664), from 20.4-31.3 C in Charlotte Harbor (7891, 16.0-34.0 C in Everglades National Park (702 1373), 19.9-33.6 C at Matecumbe Key (8001, and at 18.0-36.0 C at Jupiter Inlet (887). Springer and Woodburn (664) reported that the species was killed by cold (water temperatures of 13 C) in the Tampa Bay area, and that live individuals noted at the same time swam sluggishly. Gilmore et a1 (236) also reported the species suffering from hypothermal stress in Tampa Bay when water temperatures ranged from 6.7 to 7.7 C. Death caused by cold temperatures has been reported at temperatures of 9.6 C in Tampa Bay (1447) and at 6.0 C in Indian River Lagoon (236).

sections.heading: Salinity
sections.content: Juvenile/adults: Euryhaline, with a wider salinity tolerance than E. gula (789 891). Said to prefer lower salinities than E. gula by some (664 789 8871, but others found that it prefers higher salinities than E. gula (702 1446). Reported to be more abundant at low to intermediate salinities in the Ten Thousand Islands, and although taken at salinities from 0-35 ppt, the species was much more abundant over the range of 2-20 ppt (1054).
